wax-squish.notes: Real recording of a slime ball being squeezed in a hand, used as a stand-in for the soft inner core of the wax ball. Each slice is one soft, dull squeeze burst of 136-200 ms (centroid 2026-2734 Hz) with no sharp pops, only a few tiny micro-bursts inside the one squeeze. Picked for single-gesture shape, event SNR >= 44 dB, no clipping, source noise floor -64 dBFS; RMS -24 to -21 dBFS, spread 3.3 dB. A 4.5 kHz low-pass and 90 Hz high-pass mute the wet 4-8 kHz fizz of the original, so it is a soft mush rather than a slimy squelch. Check first: that it reads as gentle rather than slimy. The quiet gaps of the source contain a faint 54/151 Hz rumble and a weak 100 Hz-spaced buzz comb around 1.7-2.3 kHz; all are measured 40+ dB under the events. Rejected: #680447 (messy micro-pops), #448641 (spiky), #546086 (too faint), #802616 (mouth-made squishes).
wax-squish.process: Source #666969 (Freesound preview -hq.mp3 decoded to 16-bit WAV with ffmpeg at native 44100 Hz, channels averaged to mono). Filters on the whole recording before cutting: 2nd-order Butterworth 90 Hz high-pass and 4.5 kHz low-pass (scipy.signal.sosfilt, causal). Slice onset = first 1 ms block above 5% of the event's own peak, slice starts 3 ms before it; 2 ms linear fade-in, 50 ms raised-cosine fade-out, then each slice peak-normalised to 0.85 (gain below). Slices as file: file start in source s / transient onset in source s / length ms / gain dB: 01: 18.169 / 18.172 / 159 / +18.3; 02: 32.872 / 32.875 / 163 / +17.5; 03: 38.721 / 38.724 / 136 / +16.6; 04: 43.419 / 43.422 / 142 / +14.9; 05: 50.321 / 50.324 / 200 / +13.5; 06: 53.235 / 53.238 / 139 / +11.9; 07: 66.272 / 66.275 / 192 / +16.1; 08: 68.229 / 68.232 / 146 / +16.3.

jelly-land.notes: Bubbles blown through a straw into thick flour-and-water batter. Each slice is ONE bubble: a rising 'bloop' (dominant pitch climbs from about 350-650 Hz in the first half to 600-850 Hz in the second half) ending in a pop, 74-123 ms long, 62-86% of the energy in a single resonance and under 1% above 3 kHz. Used for the round, bouncy 'pong' when landing on the big soda-jelly block. Check first: the energy peaks 25-60 ms after the onset (swell then pop), so the hit lands slightly later than a click would; RMS is high (-16 to -10 dBFS, spread 5.3 dB) because the sound is tonal, so it may need turning down in the mixer. Source noise floor is -52 dBFS (borderline) but every bubble sits at least 42 dB above it and no hum lines were found. Only a 90 Hz high-pass was applied. Alternative not used (pure mouth-made plops, more synthetic): Freesound #401969.

fizz-loop.notes: Per the author: a pair of hydrophones placed in the bottom of a large glass that was then filled with carbonated water, so this is a close-up of the bubbles in the glass. The loop is a steady stretch of tiny bubble crackles (source 7.0-10.35 s, after the first seconds of pouring and the initial loud fizz): spectrum centred near 3 kHz (52% of the energy at 2-4 kHz, 16% at 4-8 kHz, about 1% above 8 kHz), discrete crackles on a soft bed, no hiss band, no narrow tonal lines, no taps inside the window. True stereo (L/R correlation about 0). 3.200 s, seamless (tiled three times: no step or level jump at the seams). Check first: being a hydrophone recording it may sound warmer or more underwater than an over-the-glass microphone. Brighter candidates were rejected as hissy (#579105, #683521, #161432) or for steady tonal whistles (#733845); #187336 and #732812 were too quiet (peaks near -40 and -50 dBFS).
fizz-loop.process: Source #240574 (Freesound preview -hq.mp3 decoded to 16-bit stereo WAV with ffmpeg at 48000 Hz). Loop body = source 7.000 s to 10.200 s (3.200 s). The next 150 ms of the source (10.200-10.350 s) are crossfaded into the first 150 ms of the body with an equal-power cos/sin curve, so the end of the file flows into its beginning. DC removed, 80 Hz 2nd-order Butterworth high-pass, both channels kept, peak-normalised to 0.7 (gain +8.4 dB).
